evidence: Cic. Fin. 1.7: sī plānē sīc verterem Platōnem
terms.comment: From one language into another: ex Graecō in Latīnum vertere (Liv. 25.39.12, Lewis & Short; Traupman 32). Plautus’s ‘barbarian’ is Latin, as a Greek would call it.

evidence: Cic. Opt. Gen. 14: nec convertī ut interpres, sed ut ōrātor (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A translation is conversiō (Traupman 32) or interpretātiō (Quint. 2.14.2, Lewis & Short; Morgan–Owens).

evidence: Cic. Fin. 1.7: locōs quidem quōsdam, sī vidēbitur, trānsferam

terms.comment: Word for word is verbum prō verbō reddere (Cic. Opt. Gen. 14) or ad verbum exprimere (Cic. Fin. 1.4, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: huic Graecē nōmen est Thēnsaurō fābulae: Philēmō scrīpsit, Plautus vertit barbarē
phrases.english: In Greek this play is called The Treasure: Philemon wrote it, Plautus translated it into barbarian

phrases.latin: cum ea, quae lēgeram Graecē, Latīnē redderem, nōn sōlum optimīs verbīs ūterer et tamen ūsitātīs
phrases.english: when I put into Latin what I had read in Greek, I used words that were not only the best but also familiar

phrases.latin: nec verbō verbum cūrābis reddere fīdus interpres
phrases.english: nor will you take care, as a faithful translator, to render word for word
